related_questions.question: What is the deadline for the US debt ceiling?

text_blocks.snippet: The U.S. debt ceiling deadline is not a fixed date, but rather a point in time when the Treasury Department is projected to exhaust its ability to meet all of the nation's financial obligations. This happens when the debt limit, which is the maximum amount the government can borrow, is reached. The debt limit was reinstated on January 2, 2025, after a suspension. The Treasury is currently using "extraordinary measures" to manage the debt, but these measures have a limited lifespan. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates that these measures will be exhausted in August or September 2025, potentially leading to a default if Congress doesn't act.

list.title: Reinstatement:

list.title: Extraordinary Measures:
list.snippet: The Treasury Department uses "extraordinary measures" (like accounting maneuvers) to continue paying bills when the debt limit is reached.

list.title: X Date:
list.snippet: The point at which the Treasury's cash on hand and extraordinary measures are exhausted is called the "X Date".

list.title: CBO Projection:
list.snippet: The CBO projects that the X Date will be reached in August or September 2025 if the debt limit is not raised.

list.title: Consequences of Default:
list.snippet: If the debt limit is not raised, the U.S. could default on its obligations, leading to significant economic consequences.

text_blocks.snippet: The debt ceiling will be reinstated on January 1, 2025, after being suspended through the end of 2024. The Treasury will then begin using "extraordinary measures" to manage the debt limit. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates that these measures will likely be exhausted in August or September 2025, at which point Congress will need to raise or suspend the debt ceiling again to avoid a potential default.
